title: Every individual credit position is its own Allocation System Instance, so onboarding an asset is a governance act
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.1.2 organizes Grove's live allocations as a three-level tree: network (A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.1.2.1, "Ethereum Mainnet"), then protocol (A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.1.2.1.1 "Centrifuge", A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.1.2.1.2 "Blackrock"), then one entry per asset — Centrifuge JTRSY, JAAA, ACRDX, and a JTRSY USDS Vault, each pointing to its **own** Instance Configuration Document.

The granularity is the claim. Grove does not hold a single "Centrifuge allocation" configured at the protocol level; it holds a separately instantiated, separately configured Primitive Instance per asset. Each therefore has its own parameters, its own operational process definition, and its own data repository.

The governance consequence is direct: because Instances live in the Artifact, **adding a new asset requires amending the Artifact**. Asset onboarding is not an operational decision made inside a risk mandate — it runs through Root Edit, and if it increases on-chain risk it also runs through the Core Council Risk Advisor (A.6.1.1.2.2.2.2.2.1.2.4). This is precisely why that section's exemptions are written per-asset-class rather than per-protocol.

Indexing by network at the top level also anticipates multi-chain deployment: the same protocol on a different chain is a different Instance under a different branch, so chain risk is never collapsed into asset risk.

The cost is throughput. An institutional credit platform that must pass a governance cycle per position is structurally slower than a fund with a mandate — which is the trade the Atlas accepts in exchange for having every exposure individually visible and individually approved.
description: Active Instances are indexed network, then protocol, then asset — Centrifuge JTRSY, JAAA, ACRDX each get a separate Instance Configuration Document rather than sharing a protocol-level entry.
